summary: The Murji'a were an early theological current that deferred (irja') judgment on those who committed major sins, holding that faith (iman) consists of belief in the heart alone and that deeds do not increase or decrease iman. Classical Sunni scholars refuted this position, holding that deeds are part of iman.
overview:
The Murji'a (Arabic: al-Murji'ah, from irja' meaning 'to defer' or 'to give hope') emerged in the first century AH as a theological response to the First Fitna and the Khawarij controversy. Where the Khawarij declared grave sinners to be disbelievers (kafirs), the Murji'a took the opposite extreme: that acts of disobedience cannot nullify faith, and that the fate of sinners is deferred entirely to Allah's judgment without any consequences in this world to their status as Muslims.

At the core of the Murji'a position is a definition of iman (faith) that restricts it to belief in the heart (tasdiq bil-qalb) or to the verbal declaration (iqrar bil-lisan), without including deeds ('amal). On this view, a person who declares faith but performs no deeds — or even commits great sins — remains a complete believer as long as belief is present internally.

The standard Sunni position, developed by scholars including Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal and later synthesized in Ash'ari and Maturidi kalam, holds that iman consists of belief in the heart, declaration with the tongue, and action with the limbs — and that these elements can increase and decrease. Good deeds increase iman; sins decrease it, but do not necessarily nullify it (against Khawarij) unless they involve clear rejection of what is known to be essential to Islam.

The Murji'a position is closely associated with certain early Hanafi theological tendencies, and later Hanafi kalam (as in the works of al-Maturidi) developed a nuanced position that acknowledged the role of deeds while still maintaining that a grave sinner remains a Muslim. Sunni scholars have distinguished between 'extreme Murji'a' (who completely excluded deeds from iman) and 'moderate Murji'a' (closer to the Hanafi theological tradition).

The Murji'a as a distinct sect had largely dissolved by the 3rd-4th century AH, with most of its theological concerns absorbed into debates within the broader Sunni kalam tradition. The concern about Murji'a-type thinking resurfaced in contemporary scholarship, with some scholars critiquing what they see as a modern 'Murji'a tendency' that minimizes the practical significance of deeds in matters of faith.
disclaimer_note: The Murji'a position — that deeds do not affect iman — was refuted by classical Sunni scholars including Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal. The school no longer exists as an organized movement. Islam.wiki covers the Murji'a historical position accurately and notes its distinction from the Sunni understanding of iman.
